subject: English
description: Common English idioms frequently asked in exams

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of the idiom: 'to hit the books'.
questions.explanation: 'Hit the books' means to begin studying seriously, often before an exam. Example — 'I've got finals next week, so I really need to hit the books.' A similar idiom is 'burn the midnight oil' (to study or work late into the night).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of the idiom: 'to let the cat out of the bag'.
questions.explanation: To accidentally or deliberately reveal information that was supposed to be kept secret. Example — 'He let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party.' Related idiom: 'spill the beans' (same meaning).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The idiom 'once in a blue moon' means:
questions.explanation: Used for an event that happens very rarely. Literally, a 'blue moon' is the second full moon in a calendar month, which occurs roughly every 2.5 years. Example — 'He visits his hometown once in a blue moon.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The idiom 'to beat about the bush' means:

options.option_text: To search carefully in an area
To avoid speaking directly about the point
To work very hard on a task

questions.explanation: To speak indirectly, avoiding the main issue. Hunters in medieval England would literally beat bushes to flush out game, which avoided the more direct (and dangerous) task of confronting the animal. Example — 'Stop beating about the bush and tell me the truth.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The idiom 'a piece of cake' means that something is:
questions.explanation: Used for tasks that are extremely easy. Example — 'The exam was a piece of cake.' Similar expressions: 'easy as pie', 'child's play', 'a cakewalk', 'a walk in the park'. The opposite would be 'an uphill battle' or 'tough nut to crack'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The idiom 'to bite off more than one can chew' means:

options.option_text: To eat in an impolite manner
To take on more than one can handle

questions.explanation: Attempting a task beyond one's ability or capacity. Example — 'By agreeing to three projects at once, he bit off more than he could chew.' Compare with 'in over one's head'. Caution is implied; it is usually said after someone has over-committed.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The idiom 'to turn a blind eye' means:

options.option_text: To look very carefully at something
To pretend not to notice something
To look in the wrong direction

questions.explanation: To deliberately ignore wrongdoing or something inconvenient. Origin is often attributed to Admiral Nelson, who reportedly put his telescope to his blind eye at the Battle of Copenhagen (1801) to ignore a signal to withdraw. Example — 'The manager turned a blind eye to the employees' lateness.'
